blocks.en: "Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and He will dwell with them... And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes; there shall be no more death, nor sorrow, nor crying. There shall be no more pain, for the former things have passed away." — Revelation 21:3-4 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "He aquí el tabernáculo de Dios con los hombres, y él morará con ellos... Y enjugará Dios toda lágrima de los ojos de ellos; y ya no habrá muerte, ni habrá más llanto, ni clamor, ni dolor; porque las primeras cosas pasaron." — Apocalipsis 21:3-4 (RVG)

blocks.en: A New Heaven and a New Earth
blocks.es_reference: Un Nuevo Cielo y una Nueva Tierra

blocks.en: The last vision of the book is its most beautiful. "Now I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away" (Revelation 21:1). The whole of the present creation will be made new; even the sun that lights this world shines by burning its fuel, and one distant day that fuel will be spent, but the believer's hope does not rest on this passing creation, for God has promised a new heaven and a new earth that will never grow old. John sees the holy city, New Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. Then a loud voice declares the heart of it all: "Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and He will dwell with them" (Revelation 21:3). And the promise that has comforted the people of God in every age of suffering is spoken: "God will wipe away every tear from their eyes; there shall be no more death, nor sorrow, nor crying. There shall be no more pain, for the former things have passed away" (Revelation 21:4). Heaven is a place of perfect joy, where the causes of every tear — sin, sickness, sorrow, separation, and death — are gone forever.
blocks.es_reference: La última visión del libro es la más hermosa. "Y vi un cielo nuevo y una tierra nueva; porque el primer cielo y la primera tierra pasaron" (Apocalipsis 21:1). Toda la presente creación será hecha nueva; aun el sol que alumbra este mundo brilla quemando su combustible, y un lejano día ese combustible se agotará, pero la esperanza del creyente no descansa en esta creación pasajera, pues Dios ha prometido un nuevo cielo y una nueva tierra que nunca envejecerán. Juan ve la santa ciudad, la nueva Jerusalén, descender de Dios del cielo, dispuesta como una esposa ataviada para su marido. Entonces una gran voz declara el corazón de todo: "He aquí el tabernáculo de Dios con los hombres, y él morará con ellos" (Apocalipsis 21:3). Y se habla la promesa que ha consolado al pueblo de Dios en toda edad de sufrimiento: "Enjugará Dios toda lágrima de los ojos de ellos; y ya no habrá muerte, ni habrá más llanto, ni clamor, ni dolor; porque las primeras cosas pasaron" (Apocalipsis 21:4). El cielo es un lugar de gozo perfecto, donde las causas de toda lágrima — el pecado, la enfermedad, la tristeza, la separación, y la muerte — se han ido para siempre.

blocks.en: Behold, I Make All Things New
blocks.es_reference: He Aquí, Yo Hago Nuevas Todas las Cosas

blocks.en: From the throne, He who sits there speaks: "Behold, I make all things new" (Revelation 21:5). He does not merely make new things; He makes all things new. Then He says, "It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End. I will give of the fountain of the water of life freely to him who thirsts" (Revelation 21:6). To all who are weary and dry, the offer still stands, full and free, to drink of the water of life without price. "He who overcomes shall inherit all things, and I will be his God and he shall be My son" (Revelation 21:7). But the same passage speaks plainly of the other destiny, for the cowardly, the unbelieving, the abominable, murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars have their part "in the lake which burns with fire and brimstone, which is the second death" (Revelation 21:8). The new creation is for those who have come to the Lamb; the lake of fire is the end of those who would not. So even in this scene of glory the call of the gospel is heard, that whoever thirsts may come and drink and live.
blocks.es_reference: Desde el trono, el que está sentado allí habla: "He aquí, yo hago nuevas todas las cosas" (Apocalipsis 21:5). No hace meramente cosas nuevas; hace nuevas todas las cosas. Entonces dice: "Hecho está. Yo soy el Alfa y la Omega, el principio y el fin. Al que tuviere sed, yo le daré gratuitamente de la fuente del agua de la vida" (Apocalipsis 21:6). A todos los que están cansados y secos, la oferta aún permanece, plena y gratuita, de beber del agua de la vida sin precio. "El que venciere heredará todas las cosas; y yo seré su Dios, y él será mi hijo" (Apocalipsis 21:7). Pero el mismo pasaje habla claramente del otro destino, pues los cobardes, los incrédulos, los abominables, los homicidas, los fornicarios, los hechiceros, los idólatras, y todos los mentirosos tienen su parte "en el lago que arde con fuego y azufre, que es la muerte segunda" (Apocalipsis 21:8). La nueva creación es para los que han venido al Cordero; el lago de fuego es el fin de los que no quisieron. Así aun en esta escena de gloria se oye el llamado del evangelio, que todo el que tenga sed venga y beba y viva.

blocks.en: The Bride, the New Jerusalem
blocks.es_reference: La Esposa, la Nueva Jerusalén

blocks.en: One of the seven angels who had the bowls now shows John the bride, the Lamb's wife. It is striking that the same kind of angel who had shown him Babylon the great harlot now shows him the holy city, for the New Jerusalem is everything Babylon was not: pure where Babylon was corrupt, faithful where Babylon was false, eternal where Babylon has fallen forever. The city descends having the glory of God, her light like a precious jasper stone, clear as crystal. She has a great high wall with twelve gates, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of Israel; and the wall has twelve foundations, and on them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb, bringing together the names of Israel’s twelve tribes and the Lamb’s twelve apostles, portraying the New Jerusalem in terms that encompass the sweep of God’s redemptive people. The city is laid out foursquare, a vast cube of pure gold like clear glass, her wall of jasper, her twelve foundations adorned with every kind of precious stone, her twelve gates each a single pearl, her street pure gold. The picture is of a city of unimaginable beauty, value, and security, the everlasting home of the redeemed.
blocks.es_reference: Uno de los siete ángeles que tenían las copas ahora muestra a Juan la desposada, la esposa del Cordero. Es notable que la misma clase de ángel que le había mostrado a Babilonia la gran ramera ahora le muestre la santa ciudad, pues la nueva Jerusalén es todo lo que Babilonia no era: pura donde Babilonia era corrupta, fiel donde Babilonia era falsa, eterna donde Babilonia ha caído para siempre. La ciudad desciende teniendo la gloria de Dios, su luz como una piedra de jaspe preciosa, diáfana como el cristal. Tiene un gran muro alto con doce puertas, y en las puertas los nombres de las doce tribus de Israel; y el muro tiene doce fundamentos, y en ellos los nombres de los doce apóstoles del Cordero, reuniendo los nombres de las doce tribus de Israel y los doce apóstoles del Cordero, retratando la nueva Jerusalén en términos que abarcan la amplitud del pueblo redimido de Dios. La ciudad está dispuesta en cuadro, un vasto cubo de oro puro semejante al vidrio limpio, su muro de jaspe, sus doce fundamentos adornados de toda clase de piedras preciosas, sus doce puertas cada una una sola perla, su plaza de oro puro. El cuadro es de una ciudad de belleza, valor, y seguridad inimaginables, el hogar eterno de los redimidos.

blocks.en: God and the Lamb Are Its Light
blocks.es_reference: Dios y el Cordero Son su Lumbrera

blocks.en: John notices what the city does not have, and each absence is a glory. "I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple" (Revelation 21:22); there is no need of a holy place to draw near to God, for God Himself is there in the midst of His people. And the city "had no need of the sun or of the moon to shine in it, for the glory of God illuminated it, and the Lamb is its light" (Revelation 21:23). The nations of the saved walk in its light, and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it. Its gates are never shut, for there is no night there and no enemy to fear. And nothing unclean, nor anyone who works abomination or a lie, will ever enter it, "but only those who are written in the Lamb's Book of Life" (Revelation 21:27). The one question of the great white throne returns here in the city of joy: whether a name is written in the Lamb's book. Those who are His enter the open gates and dwell forever in the light of God.
blocks.es_reference: Juan nota lo que la ciudad no tiene, y cada ausencia es una gloria. "Y no vi en ella templo; porque el Señor Dios Todopoderoso es el templo de ella, y el Cordero" (Apocalipsis 21:22); no hay necesidad de un lugar santo para acercarse a Dios, pues Dios mismo está allí en medio de su pueblo. Y la ciudad "no tiene necesidad de sol ni de luna que resplandezcan en ella; porque la gloria de Dios la ilumina, y el Cordero es su lumbrera" (Apocalipsis 21:23). Las naciones de los salvos andan en su luz, y los reyes de la tierra traen su gloria a ella. Sus puertas nunca se cierran, pues allí no hay noche ni enemigo que temer. Y nada inmundo, ni nadie que hace abominación o mentira, entrará jamás en ella, "sino solamente los que están escritos en el libro de la vida del Cordero" (Apocalipsis 21:27). La única pregunta del gran trono blanco regresa aquí en la ciudad de gozo: si un nombre está escrito en el libro del Cordero. Los que son suyos entran por las puertas abiertas y moran para siempre en la luz de Dios.

blocks.en: The River and the Tree of Life
blocks.es_reference: El Río y el Árbol de la Vida

blocks.en: In the midst of the city John sees a pure river of the water of life, clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life on either side, bearing twelve fruits and yielding its fruit every month, "and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations" (Revelation 22:2). What was lost in the garden of Eden is restored and surpassed, for "there shall be no more curse" (Revelation 22:3). The servants of God will serve Him and see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads, and they will reign forever and ever. This is the believer's true hope, and it reaches even to the body, for the resurrection body will be like the body of the risen Christ, who still bore the marks of the cross yet could enter a closed room, real and recognizable, transformed and glorious, no longer subject to weakness, pain, or death. There is a true account of a young man dying of a terminal illness. His pastor came to visit, and as the two sat talking the young man began to weep. The pastor took out his handkerchief and gently wiped the tears, first from one eye and then from the other. The young man smiled and said that the next time his tears were wiped away, they would be wiped away by the hand of his heavenly Father. That is the promise of these chapters made personal.
blocks.es_reference: En medio de la ciudad Juan ve un río limpio de agua de vida, resplandeciente como cristal, que sale del trono de Dios y del Cordero, y el árbol de la vida a uno y otro lado, que lleva doce frutos y da su fruto cada mes, "y las hojas del árbol eran para la sanidad de las naciones" (Apocalipsis 22:2). Lo que se perdió en el huerto del Edén es restaurado y sobrepasado, pues "no habrá más maldición" (Apocalipsis 22:3). Los siervos de Dios le servirán y verán su rostro, y su nombre estará en sus frentes, y reinarán por los siglos de los siglos. Esta es la verdadera esperanza del creyente, y alcanza aun al cuerpo, pues el cuerpo de resurrección será como el cuerpo del Cristo resucitado, que aún llevaba las marcas de la cruz pero podía entrar en un cuarto cerrado, real y reconocible, transformado y glorioso, ya no sujeto a la debilidad, el dolor, ni la muerte. Hay un relato verdadero de un joven que moría de una enfermedad terminal. Su pastor vino a visitarlo, y mientras los dos conversaban sentados el joven comenzó a llorar. El pastor sacó su pañuelo y enjugó suavemente las lágrimas, primero de un ojo y luego del otro. El joven sonrió y dijo que la próxima vez que sus lágrimas fuesen enjugadas, serían enjugadas por la mano de su Padre celestial. Esa es la promesa de estos capítulos hecha personal.

blocks.en: Behold, I Am Coming Quickly
blocks.es_reference: He Aquí, Yo Vengo Pronto

blocks.en: As the book draws to its close, the words are sealed with a solemn assurance: "These words are faithful and true" (Revelation 22:6). Three times in this chapter the Lord says, "Behold, I am coming quickly" (Revelation 22:7, 12, 20), and a blessing is pronounced on the one who keeps the words of this prophecy. When John once more falls down to worship the angel, he is again forbidden and told, "Worship God" (Revelation 22:9). The hope of the Lord's return has steadied His people in death itself. There is a true account of a man whose wife of fifty-seven years had died; as he stood at her casket and was asked whether he wished to say goodbye, he answered, "This is not goodbye; I will be seeing her again." After a long decade alone he too died, at the age of ninety-two, longing to hold her once more, and at his funeral the message was the hope of heaven. Such hope is why the book ends with an open invitation: "And the Spirit and the bride say, 'Come!' And let him who hears say, 'Come!' And let him who thirsts come. Whoever desires, let him take the water of life freely" (Revelation 22:17). Jesus calls Himself "the Root and the Offspring of David, the Bright and Morning Star" (Revelation 22:16).
blocks.es_reference: Al acercarse el libro a su fin, las palabras son selladas con una solemne seguridad: "Estas palabras son fieles y verdaderas" (Apocalipsis 22:6). Tres veces en este capítulo el Señor dice: "He aquí, yo vengo pronto" (Apocalipsis 22:7, 12, 20), y se pronuncia una bienaventuranza sobre el que guarda las palabras de esta profecía. Cuando Juan una vez más se postra para adorar al ángel, de nuevo se le prohíbe y se le dice: "Adora a Dios" (Apocalipsis 22:9). La esperanza del regreso del Señor ha sostenido a su pueblo en la muerte misma. Hay un relato verdadero de un hombre cuya esposa de cincuenta y siete años había muerto; mientras estaba de pie ante su ataúd y se le preguntó si deseaba despedirse, respondió: "Esto no es una despedida; volveré a verla." Después de una larga década solo él también murió, a la edad de noventa y dos años, anhelando abrazarla una vez más, y en su funeral el mensaje fue la esperanza del cielo. Por tal esperanza el libro termina con una invitación abierta: "Y el Espíritu y la Esposa dicen: Ven. Y el que oye, diga: Ven. Y el que tiene sed, venga; y el que quiera, tome del agua de la vida gratuitamente" (Apocalipsis 22:17). Jesús se llama a sí mismo "la raíz y el linaje de David, la estrella resplandeciente, y de la mañana" (Apocalipsis 22:16).

blocks.en: Even So, Come, Lord Jesus
blocks.es_reference: Así Sea, Ven, Señor Jesús

blocks.en: The book closes with a warning not to add to or take away from the words of its prophecy, and then with the last exchange of all. The Lord says, "Surely I am coming quickly," and the church answers from the heart, "Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus" (Revelation 22:20). So the Revelation ends not in fear but in hope. The two cities have been set before the reader, Babylon the harlot, fallen forever, and the New Jerusalem the bride, radiant forever, and the whole book asks to which city a soul belongs. It calls the church to endure through tribulation, to refuse the mark of the beast, to keep the faith of Jesus, and to long for the Lamb's return. For those who are His, the day is coming when the tired and broken body will be exchanged for one that is glorious and free, when God Himself will wipe away every tear, when the curse will be gone and death will be no more, and when the redeemed will see His face and reign with Him forever. To the grieving believer this book says that parting at the grave is not goodbye but good night, and that the next time tears are wiped away, it will be by the loving hand of the heavenly Father. "Even so, come, Lord Jesus."
blocks.es_reference: El libro se cierra con una advertencia de no añadir ni quitar de las palabras de su profecía, y luego con el último intercambio de todos. El Señor dice: "Ciertamente vengo en breve," y la iglesia responde de corazón: "Amén; sí, ven, Señor Jesús" (Apocalipsis 22:20). Así el Apocalipsis termina no en temor sino en esperanza. Las dos ciudades han sido puestas delante del lector, Babilonia la ramera, caída para siempre, y la nueva Jerusalén la esposa, radiante para siempre, y todo el libro pregunta a cuál ciudad pertenece un alma. Llama a la iglesia a perseverar en la tribulación, a rehusar la marca de la bestia, a guardar la fe de Jesús, y a anhelar el regreso del Cordero. Para los que son suyos, viene el día en que el cuerpo cansado y quebrantado será cambiado por uno que es glorioso y libre, en que Dios mismo enjugará toda lágrima, en que la maldición se habrá ido y la muerte no será más, y en que los redimidos verán su rostro y reinarán con él para siempre. Al creyente que llora este libro le dice que la despedida ante la tumba no es un adiós sino un buenas noches, y que la próxima vez que las lágrimas sean enjugadas, será por la mano amorosa del Padre celestial. "Así sea, ven, Señor Jesús."

blocks.en: "He who testifies to these things says, 'Surely I am coming quickly.' Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus! The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen." — Revelation 22:20-21 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "El que da testimonio de estas cosas dice: Ciertamente vengo en breve. Amén; sí, ven, Señor Jesús. La gracia de nuestro Señor Jesucristo sea con todos vosotros. Amén." — Apocalipsis 22:20-21 (RVG)

mc.why: The twelve gates bore the names of the twelve tribes of Israel (21:12).

mc.stem: The city's twelve foundations bore the names of:
options: The twelve apostles of the Lamb
mc.why: The twelve foundations bore the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb (21:14).

mc.stem: The New Jerusalem had no temple, because:
options: The Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple
mc.why: "The Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple" (21:22).

mc.stem: The city had no need of sun or moon, because:
options: The glory of God illuminated it, and the Lamb is its light
mc.why: "The glory of God illuminated it, and the Lamb is its light" (21:23).

mc.stem: From the throne of God and of the Lamb flowed:
options: A pure river of the water of life
mc.why: "A pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, from the throne" (22:1).

mc.stem: The tree of life bore twelve fruits, and its leaves were for:
mc.why: "The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations" (22:2).

mc.stem: In the city of God, John says there is no more:
mc.why: "And there shall be no more curse" (22:3).

mc.stem: God's servants will serve Him and will also:

mc.why: "They shall see His face, and His name shall be on their foreheads" (22:4).

mc.why: "Behold, I am coming quickly" is repeated (22:7, 12, 20).

options: Come!... let him who thirsts take the water of life freely
mc.why: "And the Spirit and the bride say, Come... take the water of life freely" (22:17).

mc.stem: Jesus calls Himself the Root and Offspring of David, and also:
mc.why: "I am the Root and the Offspring of David, the Bright and Morning Star" (22:16).

mc.stem: The book closes with the church's answer to Christ's promise to come:
options: Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus!
mc.why: "Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus!" (22:20).

sa.prompt: Describe the new heaven and new earth and God's dwelling with His people (21:1-4).
sa.model: The last vision of the book is its most beautiful. John saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away. The whole of the present creation will be made new; even the sun that lights this world shines by burning its fuel, and one day that fuel will be spent, but the believer's hope rests not on this passing creation but on the new heaven and new earth that God has promised, which will never grow old. John sees the holy city, New Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. Then a loud voice declares the heart of it all, that the tabernacle of God is with men, and He will dwell with them, and they shall be His people, and God Himself will be with them. And the promise that has comforted the people of God in every age of suffering is spoken, that God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there shall be no more death, nor sorrow, nor crying, nor pain, for the former things have passed away. Heaven is a place of perfect joy, where the causes of every tear are gone forever.

sa.prompt: What do the words "Behold, I make all things new" and the offer of the water of life mean (21:5-8)?
sa.model: From the throne, He who sits there says, Behold, I make all things new. He does not merely make new things; He makes all things new, renewing the whole creation. Then He says, It is done, I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End, and He promises to give of the fountain of the water of life freely to him who thirsts. To all who are weary and dry, the offer still stands, full and free, to drink of the water of life without price, and the one who overcomes shall inherit all things and shall be God's son. But the same passage speaks plainly of the other destiny, for the cowardly, the unbelieving, the abominable, murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars have their part in the lake which burns with fire and brimstone, which is the second death. The new creation is for those who have come to the Lamb, and the lake of fire is the end of those who would not. So even in this scene of glory the call of the gospel is heard, that whoever thirsts may come and drink and live.

sa.prompt: Describe the New Jerusalem, the bride, and how it contrasts with Babylon (21:9-21).
sa.model: One of the seven angels who had the bowls now shows John the bride, the Lamb's wife. It is striking that the same kind of angel who had shown him Babylon the great harlot now shows him the holy city, for the New Jerusalem is everything Babylon was not, pure where Babylon was corrupt, faithful where Babylon was false, and eternal where Babylon has fallen forever. The city descends having the glory of God, her light like a precious jasper stone, clear as crystal. She has a great high wall with twelve gates, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of Israel; and the wall has twelve foundations, and on them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb, bringing together the names of Israel’s twelve tribes and the Lamb’s twelve apostles, portraying the New Jerusalem in terms that encompass the sweep of God’s redemptive people. The city is laid out foursquare, a vast cube of pure gold like clear glass, her wall of jasper, her foundations adorned with every kind of precious stone, her twelve gates each a single pearl, her street pure gold. The picture is of a city of unimaginable beauty, value, and security, the everlasting home of the redeemed.

sa.prompt: How is God Himself the temple and the light of the city (21:22-27)?
sa.model: John notices what the city does not have, and each absence is a glory. He saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple; there is no need of a holy place to draw near to God, for God Himself is there in the midst of His people. And the city had no need of the sun or of the moon to shine in it, for the glory of God illuminated it, and the Lamb is its light. The nations of the saved walk in its light, and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it. Its gates are never shut, for there is no night there and no enemy to fear. And nothing unclean, nor anyone who works abomination or a lie, will ever enter it, but only those who are written in the Lamb's Book of Life. The one question of the great white throne returns here in the city of joy, whether a name is written in the Lamb's book. Those who are His enter the open gates and dwell forever in the light of God, where there is no darkness and no night at all.

sa.prompt: Describe the river and the tree of life and the end of the curse (22:1-5).
sa.model: In the midst of the city John sees a pure river of the water of life, clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life on either side, bearing twelve fruits and yielding its fruit every month, and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations. What was lost in the garden of Eden is restored and surpassed, for there shall be no more curse. The servants of God will serve Him and see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads, and they will reign forever and ever. This is the believer's true hope, and it reaches even to the body, for the resurrection body will be like the body of the risen Christ, who still bore the marks of the cross yet could enter a closed room, real and recognizable, transformed and glorious, no longer subject to weakness, pain, or death. There is a true account of a dying young man whose eyes were wet with tears as his pastor wiped them away, and who said that the next time his tears were wiped away, they would be wiped away by the loving hand of his heavenly Father. That is the promise of these chapters made personal.

sa.prompt: What is the meaning of "Behold, I am coming quickly" and the final invitation "Come" (22:6-17)?
sa.model: As the book draws to its close, the words are sealed with a solemn assurance, that these words are faithful and true. Three times in this chapter the Lord says, Behold, I am coming quickly, and a blessing is pronounced on the one who keeps the words of this prophecy. When John once more falls down to worship the angel, he is again forbidden and told to worship God. The hope of the Lord's return has steadied His people even in death. There is a true account of a man whose wife of fifty-seven years had died; as he stood at her casket and was asked whether he wished to say goodbye, he answered that this was not goodbye, for he would be seeing her again. After a long decade alone he too died at ninety-two, longing to hold her once more, and at his funeral the message was the hope of heaven. Such hope is why the book ends with an open invitation, for the Spirit and the bride say, Come, and let him who hears say, Come, and let him who thirsts come and take the water of life freely. Jesus calls Himself the Root and the Offspring of David, the Bright and Morning Star.

sa.prompt: How does the book end, and what is the church's response (22:18-21)?
sa.model: The book closes with a warning not to add to or take away from the words of its prophecy, and then with the last exchange of all. The Lord says, Surely I am coming quickly, and the church answers from the heart, Amen, even so, come, Lord Jesus. So the Revelation ends not in fear but in hope. The two cities have been set before the reader, Babylon the harlot, fallen forever, and the New Jerusalem the bride, radiant forever, and the whole book asks to which city a soul belongs. It calls the church to endure through tribulation, to refuse the mark of the beast, to keep the faith of Jesus, and to long for the Lamb's return. For those who are His, the day is coming when the tired and broken body will be exchanged for one that is glorious and free, when God Himself will wipe away every tear, when the curse will be gone and death will be no more, and when the redeemed will see His face and reign with Him forever. To the grieving believer this book says that parting at the grave is not goodbye but good night, and that the next time tears are wiped away, it will be by the loving hand of the heavenly Father.

sa.prompt: What does Revelation 21-22 teach about the believer's hope of no more tears and a new body?
sa.model: Revelation 21 and 22 set before the believer a hope that reaches to the deepest griefs of this life. God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there shall be no more death, nor sorrow, nor crying, nor pain, for the former things have passed away. Heaven is not a vague or gloomy place but one of perfect joy, where the very causes of tears, sin and sickness and separation and death, are gone forever. The hope reaches even to the body, for the resurrection body will be like the body of the risen Christ, who still bore the marks of the cross yet could enter a closed room, real and recognizable, transformed and glorious, never again to weaken, suffer, or die. The tired and broken body will be exchanged for one that is free. There is a true account of a dying young man whose tears his pastor wiped away, and who said that the next time his tears were wiped away, it would be by the loving hand of his heavenly Father. So these chapters teach that for those who belong to the Lamb, every loss will be undone, every tear dried, and the body itself raised glorious, and that death for the believer is not the end but a doorway into the unfading life of the new creation.

sa.prompt: How do the two cities, Babylon and the New Jerusalem, frame the message of Revelation?
sa.model: Revelation sets two cities before the reader, and the contrast between them frames the whole book. Babylon is the great harlot, the world in its idolatry, luxury, and cruelty, drunk with the blood of the saints, and she is fallen forever, brought down suddenly and completely under the judgment of God. The New Jerusalem is the bride, the Lamb's wife, pure and faithful and radiant, descending from God to be the eternal home of the redeemed, where God dwells with His people and wipes away every tear. It is striking that the same kind of angel shows John both the harlot and the bride, so that the two are deliberately set side by side. Each city stands for a way of life and a destiny, and the whole book asks to which city a soul belongs. To belong to Babylon is to share her sins and her doom; to belong to the New Jerusalem is to have one's name in the Lamb's Book of Life and to dwell forever in the light of God. So the message of Revelation is a summons to come out of Babylon and to enter, by faith in the Lamb, the city that will never fall.

sa.prompt: Summarize the central truth of Unit 15 and the close of the whole book of Revelation.
sa.model: The central truth of Unit 15 is that the book of Revelation ends in glory and hope, with God making all things new and dwelling forever with His people. John sees a new heaven and a new earth and the holy city, the New Jerusalem, the bride, descending from God, where God Himself is with men, where He wipes away every tear, and where there is no more death, sorrow, crying, or pain. He makes all things new and offers the water of life freely to all who thirst. The city needs no temple and no sun, for God and the Lamb are its temple and its light; from the throne flows the river of life, the tree of life heals the nations, and there is no more curse, and the servants of God see His face and reign forever. Three times the Lord promises, Behold, I am coming quickly, and the book ends with the open invitation, Come, and with the church's answer, Amen, even so, come, Lord Jesus. So the whole book calls the church to endure, to refuse the beast, to keep the faith of Jesus, and to long for the Lamb's return, assuring the grieving that parting is not goodbye but good night, and that the next tears will be wiped away by the hand of the heavenly Father.
